title: Messages as Bytes: A Layout Both Ends Agree On, and a Check That They Do

questions.question: Why not send a struct by copying its memory?
options: Copying memory is slower than writing fields one at a time: a struct of 11 bytes took 24 copies
A struct cannot contain a string, so most messages could not be sent that way
The receiver would need the same variable names as the sender, which a second program does not have
The size, padding and byte order are the compiler's and the machine's: a struct of 11 bytes of fields was 24 bytes in memory
questions.explanation: Padding and byte order are decided by the compiler and the machine. A layout that goes over a wire has to be written down field by field so both ends agree.

questions.question: How is the integer 0x1234 written as a u16, little endian?
options: 12 34, the high byte first
34 12 00 00, padded to four bytes
34 12, the low byte first
21 43, each byte's digits reversed
questions.explanation: Little endian puts the least significant byte first. The test's bytes were AB, then 34 12, then EF BE AD DE.

questions.question: A string's length field says 500 and 2 bytes follow. What should the reader do?
options: Read the 2 bytes that are there and return them as the string
Read 500 bytes, since the sender knows the length better than the reader
Wait until the other 498 bytes arrive
Fail the read and return an empty string, rather than read on into whatever lies after the message
questions.explanation: A length that came from outside may be wrong or hostile. A reader that believes it walks 498 bytes past the end of the message.

questions.question: Why does the reader keep failing after the first failed read?
options: A byte that happens to be there after a failed read is not data: what follows a failure is nonsense that looks like data
So that the caller can count how many reads failed in one message
Because the buffer is cleared on the first failure and nothing is left to read
To give the sender time to send the message again
questions.explanation: Once a read has run out, the reader no longer knows where it is in the message. Handing out the next byte would be handing out a guess.

questions.question: How does a receiver tell that a frame is for another type?
options: By the frame's length, which is different for every type
It cannot: the two programs must be built from the same source
The frame starts with a type id worked out from the message's name, and unframe answers wrong_type if it differs
By reading the payload and seeing whether the fields make sense
questions.explanation: The id is a hash of the type's name and version, so Pose2D and Pose2D/v2 differ. A mismatch is reported as a status before any field is read.

questions.question: What is the published FNV-1a value for the string a, and what is it used for?
options: 0x811C9DC5, the starting value, which is what an empty string hashes to
0xE40C292C, which is how to test an implementation of the id function against a known answer
0x00000061, the character itself, used as a short id for one letter names
0xDEADBEEF, the value the test writes as a u32, used to check the byte order
questions.explanation: A hash function is only right if it gives the published answers. Checking one known value catches a wrong constant or a wrong order of operations.
